title: Family Structure, a Key Factor Hidden in Plain Sight: The Case for Federal Reporting in Education | Institute for Family Studies
gist: AEI and IFS scholars show that in the National Survey of Children's Health, family structure out-predicts race, income, parental education, and sex for school discipline contacts, grades, and childhood depression — and argue NAEP has quietly collected household-composition data since 2013 without ever reporting it. The ask is a change in federal statistical practice: make family structure a standard reporting category across Department of Education and child-wellbeing datasets.

insights.claim: The National Assessment of Educational Progress has collected household-composition data from students continuously since 2013 — across mathematics, reading, science, civics, geography, and US history in grades four, eight, and 12 — but has never published outcomes disaggregated by family structure.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A decade of untapped federal microdata exists; whoever mines or publishes it first reframes the entire education-outcomes debate, and edtech/policy shops positioned on family-structure analytics get a first-mover narrative.
insights.quote: since 2013, NAEP has consistently and continuously collected information on family structure from students, but it has never reported it
insights.locator: Missing from all these studies and federal reports

insights.claim: The 2013 NAEP Student Questionnaire introduced a multi-select item asking children whether a mother, father, stepmother, stepfather, foster mother or other female legal guardian, or foster father or other male legal guardian lives in their home — a deliberate design choice to capture family structure comprehensively.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The instrument is granular enough to reconstruct the seven-category family taxonomy, meaning the reporting gap is a publication decision, not a data-collection limitation.
insights.quote: Do any of the following people live in your home?
insights.locator: According to the historical log NAEP has kept

insights.claim: NAEP is legally required to report only gender, race and ethnicity, socioeconomic status, disability status, and English-learner status, but is not prohibited from adding categories — so the omission of family structure is institutional choice rather than statutory constraint.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: No legislation is needed to change this — an administrative decision could flip it, which makes it a fast-moving, low-cost policy lever to watch.
insights.quote: While the latter data categories are required by law, NAEP is not necessarily prohibited from reporting student scores by additional categories.

insights.claim: Beyond not publishing it, NAEP has not made family-structure data easily accessible through the NAEP Data Explorer tool, raising the friction for independent researchers who might otherwise fill the gap.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The fallback ask — accessibility rather than official reporting — is the likelier near-term outcome and the cheaper concession for the agency to make.

insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Signals that family-structure reporting is being positioned as an administration-aligned reform, raising the odds it actually lands in this policy cycle.

insights.claim: Net of controls for race, income, parental education, sex, and age, children in non-intact or unmarried-parent homes were 47 percent more likely to have their parents contacted by school for behavioral or learning problems — a larger effect than being a boy (38 percent), being black versus white (17 percent), or being below the federal poverty line (16 percent).
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The headline number that reorders which variable deserves the intervention budget in school behavioral programs and student-support services.
insights.quote: children living in non-intact homes or with unmarried parents were 47 percent more likely to have their parents contacted by their school than were children from intact, married-parent families
insights.locator: These disparities persist when we control

insights.claim: Parental education showed no significant relationship to how often schools contacted households about behavioral or learning problems, isolating family structure as the dominant predictor of school-discipline contact.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Undercuts the standard 'educated parents fix behavior' assumption and narrows the causal search to household composition.

insights.claim: American Community Survey data show 80 percent of Asian and 69 percent of white children live with their married birth parents versus 52 percent of Latino and 30 percent of black children, meaning race-coded achievement gaps partly encode family-structure composition differences.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Any model regressing outcomes on race without household composition is likely picking up omitted-variable bias — a direct challenge to the analytic basis of race-targeted programs.

insights.claim: The Good Fathers, Flourishing Kids report found no racial divide in academic performance between white and black children from intact families in Virginia, suggesting the black-white achievement gap may be substantially a family-structure gap.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The strongest single empirical claim in the report against race-first explanations; expect it to be the focal point of both citation and attack.

insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: This is the report's ideological payload: a data argument built to redirect institutional spending away from DEI programming toward family-structure interventions.

insights.claim: The National Center for Health Statistics defined seven mutually exclusive family structures in 2010 — nuclear, single-parent, blended, unmarried biological or adoptive, cohabitating, extended, and other — and called for studying new family types, a standard that federal education reporting still has not adopted.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies

insights.so_what: A ready-made taxonomy already blessed by a federal agency means the technical objection to adopting family-structure reporting is weak.

themes.theme: The measured collapse in US student performance

insights.claim: On the 2024 NAEP, the number of fourth graders scoring 'below basic' in reading now exceeds the number reading at or above 'proficient,' with the deterioration accelerating from 2017 — before the pandemic.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The 2017 inflection undercuts the pandemic-only explanation for learning loss and points to a structural driver that predates school closures.
insights.quote: the number of fourth-grade students scoring at the lowest category of reading capability (“below basic”) now exceeds the number of fourth-grade students reading at or above NAEP “proficient” levels
insights.locator: Based on the 2024 National Assessment of Educational Progress

insights.claim: Twelfth-grade average percentile scores on the 2024 NAEP were the lowest in the history of both tests — reading since 1992 and math since 2005.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: All-time lows at the exit point of K-12 flow directly into college readiness, remediation costs, and entry-level labor quality over the next decade.
insights.locator: Similar declines are visible for older students

insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Baseline numeracy failure at this scale constrains the technical-workforce pipeline regardless of how the causal debate resolves.

themes.theme: Policy levers and the family-formation turn

insights.claim: The authors' proposed intervention is not changing families but changing expectations: teaching middle and high schoolers the 'success sequence,' under which 97 percent of young people who finish high school, work full time, and marry before having children are not poor as adults.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Curriculum-level, low-cost, and already packaged for state legislatures — the most likely concrete policy output of this research stream.

insights.claim: The share of US children living in married families bottomed at 64 percent in 2012 and rose to 66 percent by 2024, with the black share rising from 33 percent to 39 percent over the same period, alongside a declining divorce rate.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: A genuine inflection in a demographic series that ran one direction for fifty years — if durable, it changes long-run household formation, housing demand, and child-poverty projections.
insights.quote: The share of children living in married families reached its nadir at 64 percent in 2012 before climbing to 66 percent in 2024.
insights.locator: What’s more, the nation is witnessing a decline in its divorce rate

insights.claim: James S. Coleman's 1966 Equality of Educational Opportunity report already established family background as arguably the dominant driver of academic achievement, meaning federal statistical practice has ignored a 60-year-old finding.

insights.so_what: Positions the argument as restoration rather than novelty, which is a stronger rhetorical footing for changing agency practice.

insights.claim: The authors argue that publishing outcomes by family structure is itself an intervention, because it would show young people the measurable consequences of different family types and make them more proactive about their own future family formation.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Reveals the real theory of change: statistical disclosure as a behavioral nudge on marriage and childbearing decisions, not just an analytic improvement.
